# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-36 (Extended v234)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to summer Year 9, and 1784-1820 (Marseilles/Pharaon timeline). Key Paris locations: Rue Plumet, Place de la Bastille, Prison Chargemagne, Rue de l'Homme Armé No. 6, Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Champs-Élysées, Rue Saint-Honoré, Luxembourg Garden, Quai aux Fleurs, Rue du Temple, sewers (Sainte-Avoye, Louvre, Montmartre, belt, Amelot, Beautreillis), Marais, Blancs-Manteaux, Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine, Rue de l'Écharpe, Rue Pavée, Rue des Trois-Pavillons, Saint-Paul church, Rue Beautreillis near Arsenal, Grand Sewer, Rue de l'Hôpital, Père-Lachaise cemetery, Rue Mondétour, Tuileries, Rue Saint-Jacques, Rue de la Jussienne, Rue Coq-Héron. English locations: Kelmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Dungate, Ravenmere, Staveford, Wilwick, Salcombe, Wilholt, Torton, Yarlby, Gagny, Lagny, Gulhaven. Marseilles: La Canebière, Rue de Noailles, Allées de Meilhan, Rue du Grand Cours, Rue de l'Homme Armé, Medusa fountain, Palais de Justice, Accoules clock-tower, Rue Caisserie, Rue Saint-Laurent, Rue Taramis, La Consigne, Frioul, Pilon, Porto-Ferrajo, Naples, Elba, Island of Elba, Point des Catalans, Ile Ratonneau, Rue de la Loge, Catalans. **Timeline spanning 1821-1827 in Paris, 1814-1820 in Marseilles/royalist settings, 1 March 1814 for Dantès' arrest.**

## English Subplot Summary (through Chapter 36, winter Year 9)

**Established solemn promises**: Semor swore to Isric Thornmere to rebuild fallen wall at Kelmere (summer Year 9). Elra gave Matho promise to plant orchard on slope above Gulhaven; Pelia gave Fenelle promise to plant orchard above Salcombe (summer Year 7); Movie swore to Nerine promise to plant orchard above Wilholt (autumn Year 7); Yera Haskick swore to Nerine Prydenridge to repair chapel roof at Kelmere (winter Year 8); Kassa Stenson kept promise to Taric Corrley: wall at Yarlby rebuilt by harvest; Kassa's husband swore to rebuild fallen wall at Ostcombe. **Yera Haskick gave Lurald Stenworth solemn promise to carry sealed letter to Quenford (winter Year 9).** **Eldest daughter of Lura Haskick kept promise made to Nerine Prydenridge: chapel roof repair at Kelmere completed by harvest (winter Year 9). Fewyn gave Havus Stenworth solemn promise to carry a sealed letter to Salcombe (winter Year 9).**

**Chapter 34-35 migrations**: Taric Corrley moved from Dungate to Kelmere with Kassa Stenson. Luena Stenenridge's only son moved from Ostcombe to Elmhaven. Pelde Stenworth married Sebin Brackick at Torton; couple lived in Torton thereafter. Fewyn Stenworth moved from Gulhaven to Yarlby with Havus. Pelia Lindmere moved to Yarlby with Rorald Lindmere. **Havie Prydenridge found work in Staveford, moved there, and did not return to Ostcombe. Isric Thornmere followed her to Staveford within the month.** **Youngest daughter of Fewyn Stenworth was apprenticed anew and became a herbalist.** **Youngest son of Nelan Brackick was apprenticed anew and became a weaver.**

**Chapter 36 winter scenes and rumors**: Frost silvered hedges; light went early; gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps; smoke lay flat over fields; wind carried salt and tar smell; road rutted and puddled after thaw. **Bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage.** Multiple characters hummed childhood tunes while scrubbing steps (Rovus, Ismira, Isric, Yewyn, Movus). Ismira and Movus fell asleep in chairs before fire caught. Ismira laughed at story nobody else found funny. **RUMOR—Isric Thornmere told Havie Prydenridge old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar.** Movus Brackick bought ribbon at stall and regretted it; counted coins twice, came up penny short. Isric Thornmere won copper chalice from Gadrek Prydenridge at cards fairly. Isric and Havie argued with carter over oat prices. Luena gave husband of Yera Stenworth solemn promise to pay old debt owed to Haskick family. Jotho Thornmere mended torn sleeve. **Late one night Kassa Brackick confided to Davus that Stenenridge mill ledger was rewritten after flood.** Baker's boy late; line at oven grew long. Someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall. Cart loaded with turnips creaked past well. Bell for vespers rang thinly. Movus mended torn sleeve by window, said little. Rorald and Fewyn Stenworth talked of weather, harvest, lame horse. Rorald read almanac aloud, mispronouncing saints. "Will it rain?" asked repeatedly. Yewyn Haskick complained of aching back. Dog barked at nothing then went quiet. Other details: salt price repeatedly discussed; Gadrek laughed at story nobody else found funny; Rozek Stenenridge pressed jade mirror into Luvie Prydenridge's hands; Yewyn and Rozek sorted old letters by candlelight; Rorald Lindmere and others sorted letters; children chased hoop; Havus fell asleep in chair; Luvie remarked river was up again.

## Marseilles/Pharaon Subplot (1784-1820): Dantès' Arrest and Imprisonment

**Edmond Dantès' arrival, father reunion, and engagement (1814)**: Young sailor Edmond Dantès jumped into skiff at La Canebière. Shipowner Danglars observed him. Dantès ascended four flights at Allées de Meilhan, found father training nasturtiums and clematis. Dantès reported Captain Leclere dead; probable he shall become captain with M. Morrel's aid. Captain at twenty, hundred louis pay, share in profits. Emptied pockets—money expressed fears; was at Caderousse's service if needed. Observed greedy glance in Caderousse's dark eyes.

**Fernand and Mercédès tragedy**: Fernand begged Mercédès to repeat refusal; ten years of marriage dreams ruined. Mercédès replied she never encouraged hope; always said she loved him as brother; heart belonged to another. **When Fernand asked final determination, Mercédès declared: if misfortune occur to Edmond, she would ascend Cape de Morgiou and cast herself headlong from it.** Later, Dantès and Mercédès clasped in each other's arms under burning Marseilles sun. Dantès saw gloomy, pale, threatening countenance of Fernand in shadow. Young Catalan placed hand on knife. Dantès extended other hand cordially. Fernand remained mute and trembling.

**Danglars' denunciation and Caderousse's intervention**: Danglars muttered he shall get nothing from these fools; feared being between drunkard and coward. Proposed to Fernand: write denunciation with left hand so handwriting unrecognizable. Wrote letter to king's attorney naming Edmond Dantès as Murat's agent carrying letters for usurper and Bonapartist committee. Caderousse, after reading letter, comprehended all misery denunciation must entail. Exclaimed: "Yes, and that's all settled; only it will be an infamous shame." Stretched hand to reach letter; Danglars took it beyond reach, claimed jest, squeezed letter and threw into corner of arbor. Earlier, Caderousse said: "Kill Dantès! who talks of killing Dantès? I won't have him killed. He's my friend, and this morning offered to share his money with me."

**1814 wedding and feast at La Réserve (1 March morning)**: As bridal party came in sight of La Réserve, M. Morrel descended to meet it. Had repeated promise that Dantès should succeed late Captain Leclere. Edmond placed arm of affianced bride within that of M. Morrel, who conducted her up wooden steps. Guests gayly followed; structure creaked under tread. Bell for vespers rang thinly. Feast chamber spacious and lighted by windows inscribed with names of principal French cities; wooden balcony extended entire length. Entertainment fixed twelve o'clock; hour previous balcony filled with impatient guests—favored crew of _Pharaon_ and Dantès' personal friends. Mercédès, lovely as Greek girls of Cyprus or Chios, with bright flashing jet eyes and ripe coral lips, moved with light, free step. At table centre, Mercédès said "Father," pointing to father on her right; on her left she placed Fernand, "him who has ever been as a brother to me," with soft, gentle smile. Her words inflicted direst torture on Fernand; his lips became ghastly pale. Dantès' old father carried glass of topaz-hued wine to lips. Dantès explained: "Thanks to M. Morrel's influence, all difficulties removed. Permission waived usual delay; at half-past two o'clock Mayor of Marseilles will be waiting at city hall. Tomorrow he starts for Paris; four days to go, four to return, one to discharge commission, back by first of March. On second he gives real marriage feast."

**Arrest and Villefort's interrogation (1 March, during feast)**: Danglars, observing Fernand's look, saw him stagger and fall convulsively against seat near open window. Indistinct sound on stairs, measured tread of soldiery, clanking of swords. Loud voice: "I demand admittance in the name of the law!" Magistrate wearing official scarf presented himself with four soldiers and corporal. Announced: "I am bearer of order of arrest." M. Morrel felt resistance useless. Old Dantès prayed and supplicated in terms moving even the officer. Dantès surrendered. Long terrified silence followed. Old father and Mercédès remained apart absorbed in grief; at length rushed into each other's arms. Fernand appeared, poured glass of water with trembling hand, sat next to Mercédès, instinctively drew back chair. Villefort traversed antechamber, cast side glance at Dantès, took packet from gendarme, disappeared. Dantès entered pale but calm, saluting judge with easy politeness. Villefort, impassive magistrate, demanded: "Who and what are you?" Dantès replied: "I was at festival of my marriage, monsieur... I am on point of marrying young girl I have been attached to for three years." When asked political opinions, Dantès replied: "I never had any opinions. I am hardly nineteen... I love my father, I respect M. Morrel, and I adore Mercédès." Villefort gazed at ingenuous countenance, recollected words of Renée beseeching indulgence for culprit. Every word convinced him more of innocence. **Regarding Captain Leclere's death and commission: "What I ought to have done, and what everyone would have done in my place... I sailed for Island of Elba, arrived next day; found difficulty obtaining access to grand-marshal; sent ring received from captain; was instantly admitted. He questioned me concerning Captain Leclere's death; gave me letter to carry to person in Paris. I undertook it because it was what my captain bade me do."** Villefort said: "This seems truth... Give up letter from Elba, pass word you will appear if required, go rejoin friends." Villefort's face became joyous, thinking: "I hope I shall gain Renée's favor by obeying first command she imposed on me." **Villefort had destroyed the fatal letter—only proof against Dantès.**

**Villefort's remorse and decision to sacrifice Dantès (1 March evening)**: First pangs of unending torture seized Villefort's heart. The innocent victim Edmond appeared to him pale and threatening, leading Mercédès by hand, bringing remorse—not furious and terrible as ancients figured, but slow and consuming agony whose pangs intensified from hour to hour unto death. Villefort had frequently called for capital punishment on criminals whom he believed guilty, but here was innocent man whose happiness he destroyed. He was not judge but executioner. **Mercédès, hearing no news, came unobserved to inquire after him at Villefort's door.** Desirous of putting end to interview, Villefort pushed by her, closed door. But remorse not thus banished; like Virgil's wounded hero, he carried arrow in his wound. At salon, uttered sigh almost a sob, sank into chair. If sweet voice of Renée had pleaded for mercy, or fair Mercédès entered saying "In the name of God, I conjure you to restore me my affianced husband," his cold trembling hands would have signed release; but no voice broke stillness, door opened only by valet announcing travelling carriage in readiness. Villefort sprang from chair, hastily opened drawer, emptied gold into pocket, stood motionless hand pressed to head, muttered inarticulate sounds, perceived servant had placed cloak on shoulders, sprang into carriage, ordered postilions to drive to M. de Saint-Méran's. **The hapless Dantès was doomed.**

**Villefort's audience with King Louis XVIII and Noirtier's visitation (1814)**: Villefort arrived at Tuileries in dusty garb; M. de Brezé protested his attire; M. de Blacas overcame objection. King Louis XVIII sat before walnut table brought from Hartwell, carelessly listening to Blacas' warnings of Napoleon's danger. Villefort reported discovery of actual conspiracy—usurper arming three ships to land at Naples, Tuscany, or France coast; sailor arrested in Marseilles secretly visited Island of Elba and carried oral message from grand-marshal to Bonapartist in Paris preparing men's minds for return. King replied: "A conspiracy in these times is easy to meditate but difficult to conduct... If Bonaparte landed at Naples, coalition would be on foot before he reached Piombino; if Tuscany, unfriendly territory; if France, with handful of men, easily foretold result, execrated as he is. Take courage, sir; rely on our royal gratitude." King praised Villefort over minister of police, declaring royal gratitude will never forget the service. **Villefort, fearing police minister might interrogate Dantès and expose his motives, made himself friend of minister by modest demeanor, succeeding in design without forfeiting king's gratitude.**

**Villefort's subsequent advancement and Noirtier's appearance**: Villefort said to king: "Sire, the suddenness of this event must prove to your majesty that the issue is in the hands of Providence; what your majesty is pleased to attribute to me as profound perspicacity is simply owing to chance, and I have profited by that chance, like a good and devoted servant—that's all. Do not attribute to me more than I deserve, sire, that your majesty may never have occasion to recall the first opinion you have been pleased to form of me." King later mentioned General Quesnel's death, wondering if result of murder rather than suicide; Quesnel had left Bonapartist club and met unknown person at Rue Saint-Jacques. Police minister described suspect: fifty to fifty-two years old, dark, black eyes with shaggy eyebrows, thick moustache, blue frock-coat buttoned to chin, rosette of Legion of Honor at button-hole. Villefort turned red and pale hearing description, leaned on armchair, legs bending under him; but when learned the unknown had escaped, breathed again. King declared assassins shall be cruelly punished. Villefort required all coolness not to betray terror. King detached cross of Legion of Honor and gave it to Villefort.

**Noirtier's transformation and escape**: M. Noirtier—Villefort's father—entered Villefort's chamber, closed antechamber door, then bedchamber door, extending hand to surprised Villefort. Villefort watched as Noirtier cut off his compromising whiskers with firm hand before glass, took colored neckerchief instead of black cravat, put on Villefort's dark brown coat cut away in front, tried narrow-brimmed hat that fit perfectly, took up bamboo switch, walked with easy swagger characteristic of him. Noirtier left room with same calmness, and Villefort, pale and agitated, ran to window, saw him pass cool and collected by two or three ill-looking men at corner of street, perhaps there to arrest a man with black whiskers, blue frock-coat, and broad-brimmed hat.

**Imprisonment and despair (1 March afternoon/evening)**: Through Rue Caisserie, Rue Saint-Laurent, Rue Taramis to quay. Saw lights of La Consigne. Officer opened door without speaking; passage formed between soldier ranks. Reached boat held by custom-house officer. In stern-sheets between gendarmes; officer stationed at bow. Boat drifted; four sturdy oarsmen impelled rapidly towards Pilon. Chain closing port lowered; in second they were in Frioul outside inner harbor. First feeling was joy at breathing pure air—air is freedom; but soon sighed, passing before La Réserve where he had that morning been so happy. Through open windows came laughter and revelry of ball. Folded hands, raised eyes to heaven, prayed fervently. Fixed eyes upon light of Point des Catalans where Mercédès dwelt. Perceived they had got out to sea. While absorbed, they had shipped oars and hoisted sail. Rose and perceived within hundred yards black and frowning rock on which stands Château d'If. This gloomy fortress seemed scaffold to malefactor. Gendarme placed knee on chest: "Good! This is the way you keep your word as sailor! Believe soft-spoken gentlemen again! If you move, I will blow your brains out." Levelled carbine at Dantès, felt muzzle against temple. Idea of struggling crossed mind. But bethought him of Villefort's promise; death in boat from gendarme seemed too terrible. Remained motionless, gnashing teeth, wringing hands with fury. Made no resistance; like man in dream; saw soldiers on embankment; ascending steps; passed through door which closed behind him; all indistinctly as through mist. Did not see ocean, terrible barrier against freedom. Followed guide into room almost underground, bare reeking walls impregnated with tears; lamp on stool illumined apartment faintly. Jailer said: "Here is your chamber for tonight... Bread, water, and fresh straw; that is all a prisoner can wish for. Goodnight." Before Dantès could open mouth, jailer disappeared, taking lamp, leaving dim reflection of dripping walls. Dantès alone in darkness and silence—cold as shadows. With first dawn, jailer returned with orders to leave Dantès where was. Found prisoner in same position, eyes swollen with weeping. Passed night standing without sleep. Scarcely tasted food; walked round cell like wild beast in cage. One thought tormented him: during journey he sat still, whereas he might dozen times have plunged into sea and, thanks to swimming powers, gained shore, concealed himself, escaped to Spain or Italy, where Mercédès and father could have joined him. Would have been free and happy, whereas now confined in Château d'If, ignorant of father's and Mercédès' future; all because he trusted Villefort's promise. Thought was maddening. Next morning, jailer came again. Descended fifteen steps; door of dungeon opened; thrust in. Door closed; advanced with outstretched hands until touched wall; sat in corner until eyes became accustomed to darkness. Jailer was right; wanted but little of being utterly mad.

**Aftermath for others**: Mercédès met Fernand at corner of Rue de la Loge; returned to Catalans; despairingly cast herself on couch. Fernand, kneeling by side, took hand, covered with kisses she did not feel. Passed night thus. Lamp went out for want of oil; paid no heed to darkness; dawn came but she knew not it was day. Grief made her blind to all but one object—that was Edmond. M. Morrel had not readily given up fight. Learned Dantès had been taken to prison; went to all friends and influential persons; but report already in circulation that Dantès was arrested as Bonapartist agent; as most sanguine looked upon any attempt of Napoleon to remount throne as impossible, met with nothing but refusal; returned home in despair, declaring matter serious and nothing more could be done. Caderousse was equally restless and uneasy, but instead of seeking to aid Dantès, shut himself up with two bottles of black currant brandy, hoping to drown reflection. But did not succeed; became too intoxicated to fetch more drink, yet not so intoxicated as to forget what happened. With elbows on table sat between empty bottles while spectres danced in light of unsnuffed candle. Danglars alone was content and joyous—had got rid of enemy and made own situation on _Pharaon_ secure. One of those men born with pen behind ear and inkstand in place of heart. Everything with him was multiplication or subtraction. Life of man was to him of far less value than numeral, especially when by taking it away he could increase sum total of own desires. Went to bed at usual hour and slept in peace.

## Marseilles Royalist Society (1814-1820)

**Aristocratic gathering and political passions (1814)**: In mansion built by Puget in Rue du Grand Cours opposite Medusa fountain, second marriage feast being celebrated simultaneously with Dantès' nuptials. Assembly composed of flower of Marseilles society—magistrates, officers, younger family members brought up to hate Napoleon. **Marquis de Saint-Méran proposed health of King Louis XVIII, recalling patient exile of Hartwell and peace-loving King; toast excited universal enthusiasm.** Young, lovely Renée de Saint-Méran engaged M. de Villefort. **Villefort replied he would place Robespierre on scaffold in Place Louis Quinze and Napoleon on column of Place Vendôme; one equality elevates, other degrades; both revolutionary scoundrels; 9th Thermidor and 4th April 1814 lucky days for France.** Villefort's father was Girondin, later senator; Villefort disowned principles, became staunch royalist. **Marquise warned Villefort should be bound to visit offence with rigorous punishment against conspirators, as he belongs to suspected family.**

**1817-1820 developments and royal approval**: In 1817, Villefort made well-turned speech regarding father's abjuration and support of religion and order. In 1818, Comte de Salvieux cried that he said same at Tuileries when questioned by king's chamberlain. King overheard, interrupted: 'Villefort—is young man of great judgment and discretion, sure to make figure in profession; I like him much.' In 1819, Villefort expressed wish for violent dangerous diseases. **Returned to dinner, face beaming with delight; Renée regarded him with fond affection; handsome features lit with fire and animation.**

**Louis XVIII and Blacas (1814, before Villefort's audience)**: At Tuileries in little room with arched window, favorite closet of Napoleon and Louis XVIII. Blacas, who had hoped of sacrificing Villefort to own profit, said: "Sire, I am compelled to tell you that these are not mere rumors destitute of foundation which thus disquiet me; but a serious-minded man, deserving all my confidence, and charged by me to watch over the south, has arrived by post to tell me that a great peril threatens the king." King said with repressed smile: "Come in, Baron, and tell the duke all you know—the latest news of M. de Bonaparte; do not conceal anything, however serious." King quoted Virgil: "_bella, horrida bella_." Blacas described Napoleon: "Raving mad; his head becomes weaker. Sometimes he weeps bitterly, sometimes laughs boisterously, at other time he passes hours on seashore, flinging stones in water and when flint makes 'duck-and-drake' five or six times, he appears as delighted as if he had gained another Marengo or Austerlitz. Now, you must agree that these are indubitable symptoms of insanity." Minister replied: "Why, this is the way of it: Napoleon lately had review, and as two or three of old veterans expressed desire to return to France, he gave them dismissal, and exhorted them to 'serve the good king.' These were his own words, of that I am certain." Blacas said: "I say, sire, that the minister of police is greatly deceived or I am; and as it is impossible it can be the minister of police as he has the guardianship of safety and honor of your majesty, it is probable that I am in error. However, sire, if I might advise, your majesty will interrogate the person of whom I spoke to you, and I will urge your majesty to do him this honor." Minister replied: "Oh, sire, we have no occasion to invent any; every day our desks are loaded with most circumstantial denunciations, coming from hosts of people who hope for some return for services which they seek to render, but cannot."

## Marius and Cosette: Courtship to Death Vigil

**Spring Year 6 confessions through barricade**: Marius revealed orphan status, lawyer profession, father colonel-hero. Cosette revealed convent upbringing, dead mother, father M. Fauchelevent. Éponine died leading Marius to barricade. Witnessed M. Mabeuf's death, Bahorel killed. Shot broke collar bone. Vigorous hand seized him before consciousness vanished.

**Medical recovery and wedding (1 February 1833)**: Doctor declared recovery assured. Learned Cosette was not daughter of old man she called father; another Fauchelevent was real father. Dowry: five hundred eighty thousand francs, constituted legacy by dead person desiring to remain unknown. **Wedding at church of Saint-Paul: Cosette wore white taffeta petticoat, Binche guipure robe, English point veil, pearl necklace, orange flower wreath. Route: Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire. Jean Valjean rose, left unperceived during celebration.**

**Javert's death and estrangement**: Javert drowned in Seine. **RUMOR—Marius suspects Jean Valjean killed Javert in barricade.**

**Jean Valjean's revelation and withdrawal**: **Proclaimed: "I am an ex-convict."** Marius shocked, concluded Jean Valjean horrible workman but admirable work. Address changed to _you_, "Madame," "Monsieur Jean." Cosette became more gay, less tender. One day chanced to say "father." "Say Jean"—She replied: "Ah! truly, Monsieur Jean." "That is right," said he. Turned aside to wipe eyes. Complete extinction ensued. Neatly clad in black, emerged daily at same hour towards nightfall from Rue de l'Homme Armé. **He was eighty years old; before Marius' marriage, would have hardly been taken for fifty; that year had counted for thirty.** Later confined to apartment, then bed. **Revealed black jet from England, white jet from Norway; invented way of substituting slides; six hundred thousand francs made. Also managed very well with glass goods. Adjured Marius: "Have no fear, the six hundred thousand francs really belong to Cosette!"** **[Heard by God alone]: "All is over. I shall never see her more... What is frightful is to die without seeing her."** Final decline: breath intermittent; difficulty moving forearm; feet lost all movement. As wretchedness of limb increased, all majesty of soul displayed. Light of unknown world visible in eyes. **In cemetery of Père-Lachaise, vicinity of common grave, far from elegant quarter, in deserted corner beside old wall, beneath great yew tree over which climbs wild convolvulus, amid dandelions and mosses, lies stone.**

## Thénardier's Blackmail and Marius's Confrontation

**Thénardier's discovery and exposure**: Through daughter Azelma tracking married pair, discovered Cosette was Madame la Baronne Pontmercy. **Offered to drive individual from family who has no right there; claimed twenty thousand francs as price.** **Wore black cloth coat, silk waistcoat, boots, green glasses, plastered gray hair. With agility of monkey, tore off spectacles, withdrew two quills from nose, took off face as man takes off hat.**

**Marius's confrontation and evidence**: Revealed Javert's suicide facts announced in _Moniteur_ 15th June, 1832: Javert reported to prefect that, having been taken prisoner in barricade of Rue de la Chanvrerie, he owed his life to magnanimity of insurgent who, holding him under pistol, fired into air instead of blowing out his brains. **Marius possessed evidence, certain date, irrefragable proof. "You are an infamous wretch! you are a liar, a calumniator, a villain... you have only succeeded in glorifying him. And it is you who are the thief! And it is you who are the assassin! I saw you, Thénardier Jondrette, in that lair on the Rue de l'Hôpital."** Offered twenty thousand francs total, ordered him to America with daughter; wife dead. **The moral wretchedness of Thénardier was irremediable. He was in America what he had been in Europe. With Marius' money, Thénardier set up as slave-dealer.**
